intro.text: A number sign (#) is used with this entry because of evidence that autosomal recessive severe congenital neutropenia-14 (SCN14) is caused by homozygous or other biallelic mutation in the CSF3 gene (138970) on chromosome 17q21.1.

checks.claim: Autosomal recessive severe congenital neutropenia-14 (SCN14) is caused by homozygous or other biallelic mutation in the CSF3 gene.
checks.evidence_quote: Our results suggest that CSF3 deficiency in humans causes a novel autosomal recessive form of SCN.
checks.explanation: Paper reports biallelic inactivating CSF3 variants causing a novel AR SCN; the SCN14 designation is OMIM nomenclature.

checks.claim: The CSF3 gene is located on chromosome 17q21.1.
checks.evidence_quote: Here, we describe three patients from two families each segregating a different biallelic inactivating variant in CSF3 with SCN.
checks.explanation: Chromosomal location is standard nomenclature, not stated in the abstract, but accepted under the nomenclature rule.

paragraphs.text: Autosomal recessive severe congenital neutropenia-14 (SCN14) is a form of severe congenital neutropenia caused by complete deficiency of granulocyte colony-stimulating factor (G-CSF), which is encoded by the CSF3 gene (Khouj et al., 2023; Almannai et al., 2026). Biallelic inactivation of the receptor gene, CSF3R, had already been established as a cause of SCN. Khouj et al. (2023) were the first to attribute a Mendelian disease to CSF3.

checks.evidence_quote: Complete deficiency of CSF3 as a result of nonsense-mediated decay (NMD) could be demonstrated on RT-PCR using skin fibroblasts-derived RNA.
checks.explanation: Complete CSF3 (G-CSF) deficiency causing SCN is stated.

paragraphs.text: Lieschke et al. (1994) generated G-CSF-deficient mice by targeted disruption of the G-CSF gene in embryonal stem cells. The G-CSF -/- mice were viable, fertile, and superficially healthy. However, they had chronic neutropenia, with peripheral blood neutrophil levels at 20 to 30% of wildtype. Heterozygous mice had intermediate neutrophil levels, which the authors suggested reflected a gene-dosage effect. In G-CSF -/- marrow, granulopoietic precursor cells were reduced by 50%, and granulocyte, macrophage, and blast progenitor cells were also reduced. Mature neutrophils were still present in blood and marrow. A single dose of G-CSF mobilized fewer neutrophils into the circulation in the knockout mice. G-CSF treatment reversed the defect: 1 day of treatment brought circulating neutrophils up to normal levels, and after 4 days the marrows of knockout and wildtype mice were morphologically indistinguishable. The G-CSF -/- mice had a markedly impaired ability to control Listeria monocytogenes infection, with a diminished rise in blood neutrophils, a delayed rise in monocytes, and reduced infection-driven granulopoiesis. Lieschke et al. (1994) concluded that G-CSF is indispensable for maintaining normal steady-state neutrophil production, and they also implicated it in emergency granulopoiesis during infection.
